content: Infectious substances, including genetically modified organisms (GMOs), classified as Dangerous Goods in Excepted Quantities, can be packaged in primary receptacles containing these substances. When such small quantities of dangerous goods are packed with infectious substances in compliance with packing instructions P620 or P650, no additional requirements from the UN Model Regulations need to be fulfilled. An overpack is a container used by a single shipper to consolidate one or more packages into a single handling unit for easier transport and storage. If dry ice is used to maintain the temperature of the contents, the overpack may consist of insulated vessels or flasks that allow the safe dissipation of carbon dioxide gas. When an overpack is employed, all required marks and labels on the packages inside must also be displayed on the outermost layer of the overpack unless they are clearly visible through transparent wrapping. Additionally, the word OVERPACK must be marked on the overpack in letters at least 12 mm high. Before returning empty packaging to the consignor or sending it elsewhere, it must be disinfected or sterilized to eliminate any potential hazards. Any labels or markings indicating that the packaging previously contained infectious substances must be removed or obliterated. If the packaging is reused, the shipper must ensure that all marks and labels accurately reflect the current contents and not the substances it previously contained. Stabilizers used to preserve biological agents may sometimes inactivate the agent, rendering it non-infectious to humans or animals. Proper marking and labeling of packaging materials are essential to provide information about the contents, the nature of the hazard, and the packaging standards applied. All marks and labels must be clearly visible and not obscured by other labels or markings. For example, when dry ice is used as a coolant, the UN number and proper shipping name of the coolant must be provided, followed by the words AS COOLANT. The net quantity of the coolant must also be indicated, as it determines how long the infectious substance can be preserved during transit. In some cases, the net quantity of dry ice may need to be replenished during transit to maintain the cold chain over extended journeys. The net quantity of the infectious substance is also critical for biosafety and biosecurity purposes, as well as for assessing risks in the event of spillage or leakage. For Category A infectious substances, the UN packaging symbol and certification marks must be displayed. If an overpack is used, these marks will not appear on the overpack itself. The name and telephone number of a responsible person knowledgeable about the shipment must also be provided. For Category B infectious substances, specific marks and labels must be used, including the proper shipping name BIOLOGICAL SUBSTANCE, CATEGORY B in letters at least 6 mm high, displayed adjacent to the mark. Hazard labels are required for all packages containing Category A infectious substances. These labels must display three crescents superimposed on a black circle in the upper half of a diamond, with the words INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE and In case of damage or leakage, immediately notify Public Health Authority in black on a white background. The number 6 must appear in the bottom corner. For packages containing Class 9 substances, such as dry ice, a miscellaneous dangerous goods hazard label is required, featuring seven vertical stripes and the number 9 in the bottom corner. For compressed gases like liquid nitrogen, a non-flammable, non-toxic gas hazard label is required, showing a gas cylinder symbol and the number 2 in the bottom corner. Handling labels, such as orientation arrows, are required for packages containing liquids exceeding 50 mL in primary receptacles. These labels must show two arrows indicating the upright position and must be placed on two opposite vertical sides of the package. For packages transported by air, a Cargo Aircraft Only (CAO) label is required if the quantity exceeds the limits for passenger aircraft. Cryogenic liquid warning labels are necessary for substances like liquid nitrogen, except when specialized insulated packaging, such as dry shippers, is used. Documentation for the shipment of infectious substances must include a Dangerous Goods Transport Document (DGTD) for Category A substances and certain medical or clinical wastes. However, Category B substances packaged according to instruction P650 are exempt from this requirement. Electronic data processing (EDP) or electronic data interchange (EDI) may be used as an alternative to paper documentation with carrier pre-approval, but a paper copy must always be available upon request. The DGTD must include the shipper's and receiver's information, a description of the dangerous goods, the type and net quantity of the goods, and any additional information required by applicable regulations.
